analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax on large inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill gathered 155 cosponsors, but the House Ways and Means Committee never acted on it and it died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal estate tax, the tax owed on very large inheritances, and the related tax on transfers that skip a generation. It would also cut the top gift tax rate to 35% and reset the lifetime gift exemption at $10 million. The estate tax only applies to estates above roughly $11.7 million per person ($23.4 million per married couple) in 2021, so the benefits would go almost entirely to the heirs of the largest fortunes.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates — the few hundred to few thousand families each year whose estates exceed the exemption — would pay no estate tax, which can run up to 40% on amounts above the exemption. Large family-owned businesses and farms in that size range would also be spared, though most farms and small businesses already fall below the threshold. Wealthy individuals planning large lifetime gifts would gain from the lower 35% gift tax rate.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax for anyone dying after enactment, ending a tax of up to 40% on estate value above roughly $11.7 million per person.
Repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which applies when wealth passes directly to grandchildren, another route for very large dynastic fortunes.
Cuts the top gift tax rate from 40% to 35% and sets the lifetime gift exemption at $10 million with inflation adjustments, reducing the tax on very large lifetime transfers.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would lose the revenue the estate tax brings in, a cost that falls on other taxpayers through higher deficits or offsetting taxes. The benefit is concentrated among a very small number of the largest estates, so the loss to the Treasury is shared by everyone else.

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates one of the most progressive taxes in the code — one that only the largest estates ever owe — and shifts the lost revenue onto other taxpayers or the deficit.
The bill is not just repeal: it also cuts the gift tax rate to 35%, lowering the tax on very large lifetime transfers, which can serve as a route around taxation of wealth during life.

Supporters' farm and small-business concerns are narrower than they appear, since current exemptions already shield estates up to roughly $11.7 million per person, well above the size of most family farms and businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would flow almost entirely to the heirs of multimillion- and billion-dollar estates, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across everyone else. There is no meaningful benefit to households below the very top, and the gift-tax cuts extend the windfall to transfers made during life.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Jason Smith of Missouri introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act on March 9, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill attracted 155 cosponsors — 154 Republicans and 1 Democrat — but the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.
The last action in the record is the referral to Ways and Means; no markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax remains in place and the Treasury keeps the revenue it collects from the largest estates; heirs of the wealthiest fortunes did not get the repeal they sought.

for.name: Rep. Jason Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act and recruited cosponsors for it.

for.name: 154 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a large but almost entirely Republican roster of support.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing, markup, or vote; it sat after referral and expired at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Of 155 cosponsors, 154 were Republicans and 1 was a Democrat, and with Democrats holding the House majority and the Ways and Means chairmanship, the bill never advanced past its referral.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated a tax that only the largest estates — those above roughly $11.7 million per person — ever owe. Its failure means those fortunes continue to face the estate tax, while the revenue stays with the Treasury.

industries.industry: Family farms and large family-owned businesses
industries.note: These estates would have been spared the estate tax, but current exemptions already shield all but the largest such operations, so the practical gain is limited to a small subset.
Repeal would have reduced demand for complex estate and gift planning among very wealthy clients; the industry's interest in keeping the tax runs alongside the Treasury's.
